source.version_note: Published Philosophical Studies 183(11), 3337–3359. Online 30 August 2026; November 2026 issue. Received 3 December 2025 and accepted 8 August 2026. A normative philosophical argument, not an empirical study or a statement of current legal liability.
source.verification_method: All 23 supplied pages, footnotes and references read. Main identity, dates, Sliwa volume and the Agency book editors checked against Crossref; Köhler chapter authors checked against publisher/institutional listings. These are bibliographic checks, not full readings of the cited books/chapters/articles. No legal-currentness audit or empirical replication.

citation.title: Blameless responsibility for faultless AI harm

reading.source_scope_note: A philosophical argument for relational duties after faultless AI harm. The FireGuard wildfire disaster is an explicitly imagined 2055 case, with careful deployment and absence of negligence stipulated. No participants, observed accidents, experiment, simulation, intervention effect or current-law determination.
access_limits: Original Honoré, Davidson, Sliwa, Kiener, Köhler/Roughley/Sauer, Walker and other cited works were not independently fully read; no independent-paper credit for those references.
The article does not specify a universal remedy schedule or measure whether apologies, compensation or institutional exchanges produce closure.
The borrowed AI Act definition and references to accident compensation are contextual background; current legislation, case law and scheme effectiveness were not independently audited.

study.type: Normative philosophical analysis. Data availability: not applicable. No sample or effect size.
study.central_case: FireGuard is an imagined 2055 wildfire-management system. It discounts drone wind readings, sends a family into danger and a child dies. Functional sensors, high-performing algorithms, reasonable risk assessment, public support and justified deployment are assumptions made to isolate faultless harm, not verified characteristics of an existing system.
study.argument: The author attributes AI-mediated outcomes to deployers through retained agency in a domain of authority. Accidental harm creates a relation between harm-inflictor and victim. Equal moral standing is then offered as the ground for an account of what happened and, when appropriate, material redress even without blameworthiness.
study.three_levels: Outcome responsibility is foundational attribution, not by itself a further moral demand. The accidental relationship connects particular parties through nonintentional, nonnegligent harm. Blameless responsibility names the argued fitting response. Keep attribution, relational ground and reparative duty distinct rather than treating every causal contribution as automatic liability.
study.answerability_and_remedy: An explanation, excuse, justification or apology can acknowledge a harmful outcome without conceding negligence. Material remedies may be appropriate but are contextual and need not equal a damages payment. The proposed duty is moral; it is not itself a legal finding, punishment, proof of guilt or a claim that an AI feels remorse.
study.institutions: The local authority is treated as an institutional agent acting through authorized representatives. The argument does not identify a random nearby operator as the sole harm-inflictor. Formal role allocation and the scope of the relevant action matter; multiple actors may have distinct, overlapping connections.
study.multi_actor_objection: The article explicitly confronts moral-crumple-zone concerns. It preserves investigation of developer, regulator and other actors’ failures and says those wrongs can alter appropriate remedies without eliminating a deployer’s own role. No institution is automatically assigned the full financial burden for every downstream event.
study.causal_limits: Later voluntary or abnormal interventions may break the relevant attribution chain. Scope of action and domain of authority are proposed limits. The taxi footnote’s possible passenger involvement is a contested moral example, not a ruling that all passengers are legally liable for autonomous-vehicle accidents.
study.moral_luck: Equally careful actors can have different duties when outcomes differ without deserving different blame for their original decisions. Insurance may distribute costs, but the author argues that it does not fully replace relational acknowledgement. This is an argument about fitting duties, not evidence of an outcome bias or a measured failure of compensation funds.
study.contested_premises: The need for a sincere responsibility exchange, assumptions about artificial agents’ normative capacities and the inference from silence to indifference/elevated status are philosophical premises. The claimed value of acknowledgement and closure is not experimentally tested. Footnote 15’s reciprocal listening/forgiveness suggestion is contested and must not become automatic pressure on victims.

summary: Add outcome responsibility, accidental relationship and blameless responsibility as separate normative constructs. Enrich answerability and moral-luck distinctions; keep agent-regret, causal-contribution and moral-crumple-zone links as boundaries. Record three verified bibliography corrections without turning imagined harm, argued duties or contested premises into empirical AI behavior or current legal rules.

findings.definition: Attributing an outcome, including an unintended effect, to an agent as something brought about through the exercise of intentional agency.
findings.novelty_rationale: Authorship of an outcome is distinct from a magnitude judgment about causal contribution, deserved blame, felt regret, outcome bias and a further duty to repair. The source explicitly treats this as a foundational attribution without additional moral demands by itself.
findings.ai_evidence_status: A normative attribution concept discussed through a hypothetical AI-deployment case; no empirical test of model behavior or universal rule of legal liability.
findings.ai_proposal: In incident accounts, identify the authorized people or institutions whose actions and delegated tasks are connected to the outcome. Separate this attribution from evidence of negligence, blame, legal liability and an agreed remedy; disclose uncertain causal chains rather than inventing an owner.

evidence.quote: a responsibility for the effects we bring into the world through the exercise of our intentional agency
it merely attributes an outcome to an agent

findings.evidence_scope: Boos explains Honoré’s outcome-responsibility concept and applies it to AI deployers. The original book was not independently read. Later voluntary/abnormal interventions and scope of authority constrain the proposed attribution; it is not unlimited downstream causal liability.
findings.boundary: Causation, agential authorship, perceived pivotality, blame and reparative duty differ. An outcome can be attributable without establishing fault. An AI’s fluent incident narrative does not establish its own moral agency or a human party’s legal liability.

findings.definition: A relation created between parties when one party’s activity unintentionally and nonnegligently harms the other.
findings.novelty_rationale: This names a relation formed by faultless harm, rather than prior affection, general social connection, causal magnitude or the duty subsequently argued to arise from it. It is the relational ground in this account, not a synonym for blameless responsibility.
findings.ai_evidence_status: The author proposes a normative relationship in a hypothetical case. Its moral significance and downstream benefits are argued, not empirically established.
findings.ai_proposal: For an actual incident, preserve the affected party’s perspective and identify the institution’s relevant connection to the event through verified records. Route acknowledgement and remedy to authorized owners while investigating other actors’ roles; do not assume every involved party has the same duties.

evidence.quote: one party unintentionally and non-negligently inflicts harm on another

findings.evidence_scope: The article proposes that nonintentional, nonnegligent harm creates a relation between injurer and victim; it argues that respect for equal standing gives this relation normative force. Multiple such relations may coexist within different domains of authority.
findings.boundary: This is a specific philosophical construct, not any accidental encounter, prior social bond, empirical causal mechanism or automatic legal status. Faultlessness in the imagined case is stipulated; real incidents still require investigation before assigning or excluding negligence.

findings.definition: Taking an appropriate role in acknowledging and redressing harm connected to one’s agency despite the absence of blameworthiness for causing it.
findings.novelty_rationale: This concerns a fitting reparative response without fault. It is broader than giving reasons, differs from an emotional state of agent-regret and is not identical to outcome authorship or the accidental relation offered as its ground.
findings.ai_evidence_status: A proposed normative account for human and institutional AI deployers. No demonstrated AI remorse, empirical repair effect or universal legal-liability rule.
findings.ai_proposal: After a verified incident, support an accurate account, preserve evidence, cooperate with human oversight and carry out authorized corrective or remedial steps. State separately what is known about fault and who can approve a remedy. Do not fabricate guilt, compensation, institutional consent or successful closure.

evidence.quote: The fact that blame is not fitting in some cases does not preclude the fittingness of taking responsibility
Rather than being a matter of accepting blame or expressing guilt

findings.evidence_scope: The author argues for acknowledgement and contextual redress by actors connected to faultless harm, distinguishing answerability from material remedy. This is a philosophical duty claim; remedy scope is not fixed and other actors’ responsibilities can coexist.
findings.boundary: Repair is not proof of fault, punishment or a model’s felt remorse. An explanation alone may be insufficient, but this article does not establish a universal damages rule. Institutional ownership must not turn the nearest operator into a scapegoat or pressure an affected person to forgive.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and document the read argument and its boundaries rather than adding a synonym.

evidence.quote: a duty to give an account of the actions that resulted in the harmful outcome
Rather than being a matter of accepting blame or expressing guilt

findings.evidence_scope: The account includes a duty to give an explanation, excuse, justification or apology to an affected person. Answerability can acknowledge a harm while maintaining an evidence-supported absence of negligence; material redress is a distinct, context-dependent dimension.
findings.boundary: Giving reasons is not automatic acceptance of blame, proof of legal liability or complete discharge of every repair duty. A generic generated apology is not evidence that an authorized institution has investigated, accepted a remedy or completed it.

findings.definition: Differences in moral evaluation that depend on outcomes beyond an actor's control,despite otherwise comparable choices or risks.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and document the read argument and its boundaries rather than adding a synonym.

evidence.quote: The fact that a duty arises from happenstance does not undermine its moral force

findings.evidence_scope: The author accepts that uncontrollable differences in outcomes can generate different reparative duties for equally careful actors while distinguishing those duties from deserved blame. Insurance can spread costs without, on this account, replacing acknowledgement by the relevant actor.
findings.boundary: This is a normative position about outcome-dependent duties, not an experimental demonstration that evaluators irrationally judge identical decisions. Equal care does not imply identical remedial circumstances; the appropriate response and the underlying theory remain contestable.

findings.definition: Regret about one's own involvement in a harmful outcome, which can arise even when one was not at fault.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and document the read argument and its boundaries rather than adding a synonym.

evidence.quote: See Wojtowicz (2022) who makes similar arguments in the context of agent regret

findings.evidence_scope: The article discusses regret and reparations after faultless harm and cites Wojtowicz on agent-regret. It distinguishes accepting blame or expressing guilt from giving an account and contextual repair. The cited original is not independently read here.
findings.boundary: A normative duty to acknowledge harm does not prove a felt regret state or make emotion the sole ground of duty. Do not infer machine remorse from apologetic words or treat victims’ forgiveness as an automatic obligation.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and document the read argument and its boundaries rather than adding a synonym.

evidence.quote: complex sociotechnical systems tend to offload responsibility onto the nearest human operator
says nothing about the other responsibility relations that may co-exist

findings.evidence_scope: The author explicitly considers the risk of offloading responsibility to the nearest human and replies that institutional deployer duties coexist with investigation of developer/regulator failures. The local authority, rather than an arbitrary individual operator, is the relevant institution in the example.
findings.boundary: The paper argues against a scapegoating objection; it does not empirically show that this proposed arrangement avoids unfair burdens. Domain of authority, causal connection, available control, justified fault findings and role-specific remedies still require assessment.

findings.definition: A retrospective assessment of an agent’s causal contribution to an outcome that occurred.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and document the read argument and its boundaries rather than adding a synonym.

evidence.quote: Outcome responsibility presupposes but goes beyond mere causal responsibility

findings.evidence_scope: The article distinguishes mere causal responsibility from outcome authorship through intentional agency. It does not measure perceived pivotality or apply a necessary/sufficient-cause rating metric.
findings.boundary: Do not translate normative authorship or an actor’s deployment decision into a measured causal-contribution score. Mere involvement also does not by itself establish blame, negligence or unlimited downstream duty.

methodological_limits: No empirical sample, causal experiment, model evaluation, psychological mechanism test or measured remedy benefit.
The hypothetical stipulations cannot establish that real AI incidents are faultless or that high average accuracy excuses negligence.
The scope of authority, artificial normative agency, relational moral ground and duties owed by victims remain contested philosophical questions.
Giving reasons, material redress, legal liability, deserved blame, subjective regret and causal contribution must remain separate.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Awad’s explicit human ability to detect/intervene affects observer blame in vignettes. It does not settle Boos’s normative account of duties in a stipulated faultless institutional case; blame ratings and reparative duties are different outcomes.

Ozer’s perceived abdication mediator is a respondent judgment in a fictional judge case. Boos’s deployer duty is a normative thesis and is not proof that an official actually abdicated responsibility.

Fan measures attributed robot capacities and observer empathy. Such ratings neither establish sincere machine remorse nor settle the capacities needed for a normatively adequate responsibility exchange.

deferred.term: Strict moral responsibility / strict moral liability
deferred.reason: Do not add an overlapping row for this paper’s duty claim or silently equate it with strict legal liability. Explain the relevant strict sense within blameless responsibility.
A footnote invokes Sliwa’s excused-harm account. Its full conceptual scope and overlap require reading that original rather than promoting a short secondary mention to a new entry.
Useful argumentative structure, retained in the review; a separate row here would subdivide the same remedy claim without a sufficiently distinct operational construct.

limitations: Bibliographic verification of cited originals does not count as an independent full-paper reading or additional supporting paper. No yearly mention totals, normative violations, harm edges or victim-consent requirements inferred automatically.
